extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (discrete math / set theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked proofs for showing sets are countable/uncountable and for constructing one-to-one/onto maps (including Cantor's theorem, diagonalization, Cantor–Schroeder–Bernstein). Focuses on proof strategies, constructions, and common proof techniques used in undergraduate set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonalization method
rubrics_metrics.description: The method used in the proof of Cantor's theorem: arrange membership answers in a table, read the boxed answers along the diagonal and reverse them to obtain a set D that differs from every f(n) at the n-th position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define D = { n ∈ Z+ | n ∉ f(n) }. The diagonal row specifying D differs from every row (every f(m)) in at least one position (the m-th), so D cannot equal any f(m). Figure and boxed-diagonal illustration help; this is the core constructive step showing no onto map exists from Z+ to P(Z+).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove non-surjectivity by explicit counterexample set
rubrics_metrics.description: To show there is no onto function f: Z+ → P(Z+), explicitly construct a subset D of Z+ (e.g., D = { n | n ∉ f(n) }) and prove D ∉ Ran(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexpress 'f is not onto' as '∃D ∈ P(Z+) ∀n ∈ Z+ (D ≠ f(n))' and provide the particular D. Use case analysis (n ∈ f(n) or n ∉ f(n)) to prove D differs from each f(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexpress negative goals as positive statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the target is to prove 'f is not onto', restate it positively as the existence of a set D such that for every n, D ≠ f(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the logically equivalent positive formulation to guide a constructive argument (choose an explicit D) rather than attempting a direct negative proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis on an arbitrary element
rubrics_metrics.description: Let an element n be arbitrary and prove a property by splitting into exhaustive cases (e.g., n ∈ f(n) vs n ∉ f(n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (Cantor's theorem, proofs of injectivity/surjectivity). Make cases exhaustive and in each case derive the desired inequality/equality; this yields a general proof for arbitrary n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define injective maps via digit/sequence encodings
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a function f: P(Z+) → R (or similar) by encoding membership as digits of a real number (e.g., f(A)=0.d1d2d3... where dn = 3 if n∈A and 7 otherwise) and show injectivity by differing at the earliest differing index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure decimal expansions are chosen to avoid ambiguity (e.g., avoid repeating-9 issues), then prove f(A) ≠ f(B) by exhibiting an index where membership differs so digits differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present strategy / scratch work before formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the proof strategy informally (scratch work) before giving the formal proof to help readers understand tricky constructions (as done before Cantor's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors separate heuristic reasoning from the formal proof and note that the heuristic won't appear in the formal write-up; this helps readers follow the motivation behind definitions (like choice of D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure functions are well-defined
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a piecewise or inverse-based function (e.g., using g^{-1}), verify the inverse is defined on the domain elements where it is used (e.g., show elements are in Ran(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In CSB construction, define R = Ran(g) so g^{-1} makes sense on R; check domains explicitly before using inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct bijections from injections via Cantor–Schroeder–Bernstein
rubrics_metrics.description: Given injections f: A → B and g: B → A, split A into subsets X and Y (constructed via a recursive sequence of sets) and define h(a) = f(a) for a∈X and h(a) = g^{-1}(a) for a∈Y to obtain a one-to-one onto map h: A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define A1 = A an(g) and An+1 = g(f(An)); let X = ⋃_{n≥1} An and Y = A  ackslash X. Prove h is one-to-one by analyzing cases a∈X vs a∈Y, and prove onto by considering whether g(b)∈X or g(b)∈Y for arbitrary b∈B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recursion/induction to build sequences of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Define sequences of sets recursively to partition domains (e.g., Ai+1 = g(f(Ai))) and take unions to form the parts used in constructions (X = ⋃Ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show by construction that each Ai must lie in the appropriate part (e.g., X), and use properties of f and g to deduce necessary membership relations; recursion organizes an infinite iterative process needed for the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove one-to-one and onto separately with clear case breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a constructed function h is bijective, give separate proofs that h is injective and surjective, each using case analysis tailored to the function's piecewise definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In injectivity proofs, assume h(a1)=h(a2) and derive contradictions unless a1=a2 by splitting into cases (a1∈X vs a1∈Y). For surjectivity, given b∈B consider g(b)∈X or g(b)∈Y to find a preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply well-ordering principle to choose integers in inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the well-ordering principle on a nonempty subset of N to obtain the smallest element and derive existence of rationals between reals (Lemma 7.3.4 uses this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the set S = { j ∈ N | m + j/k > x } and take its least element to produce a rational j/k between x and y; justify j>0 and related inequalities carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use injections to compare cardinalities (dominance relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ≼ B (B dominates A), give a one-to-one function f: A → B. Use known injections or construct explicit ones to deduce dominance relations between familiar sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitivity of injections and composition arguments are used to chain relations; exercise examples show deriving A ≼ B from constructed maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit examples to illustrate abstract constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete examples (e.g., A = set of even integers gives f(A)=0.373737..., P = set of primes gives f(P)=0.37737373337...) to illustrate how encoding constructions work and to build intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples make the general construction clearer and demonstrate injectivity/uniqueness properties in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design exercises that encourage imitation of proofs and generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises often direct students to 'imitate the proof of Theorem 7.2.5' or 'use this method to find a bijection' so students practice applying the same technique in varied contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints in exercises point to the appropriate earlier construction; students should abstract the pattern (e.g., diagonalization or CSB construction) and adapt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical exposition practice: separate informal motivation from formal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide informal 'scratch work' or motivational paragraphs explaining the choice of constructions, then present the concise formal proof; reassure readers that the heuristic isn't required in the formal write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves readability: give the idea first, then the formal argument. Invite readers to reread the heuristic after seeing the proof if they found it hard to follow initially.
